seoDescription: Learn how to build a completely free, local RAG chatbot using Flowise and Ollama. This tutorial guides you through setting up Ollama on your machine to run open-source large language models (LLMs) like Llama 2 at no cost. You'll see how to integrate Ollama with a local Flowise instance, starting with a basic conversational chain and then advancing to a powerful RAG chatbot. Discover how to scrape website data and query it, creating a private and cost-effective AI solution running entirely on your hardware.

chapters.title: Introduction: Free Local Chatbots with Ollama
chapters.description: This chapter introduces the concept of building a free, local RAG chatbot using Flowise and Ollama to avoid the costs associated with cloud-based LLMs.

chapters.title: Installing and Running Your First Local LLM
chapters.description: Learn how to download and install Ollama, then use the terminal to download and run your first local language model, Llama 2.

chapters.title: Serving Ollama for Flowise Integration
chapters.description: This section covers how to run Ollama as a local server using `olama serve`, making it accessible as an API for tools like Flowise.

chapters.title: Building a Basic Conversational Chatbot in Flowise
chapters.description: Follow a step-by-step guide to create a simple conversational chatbot in Flowise using the ChatOlama node connected to your local model.

chapters.title: Building the Local RAG Chatbot Chain
chapters.description: Start building a RAG chatbot by setting up a Conversational Retrieval QA Chain, the ChatOlama model, a vector store, and the Olama embeddings node.

chapters.title: Adding Data and Testing the RAG Chatbot
chapters.description: Learn to add a web-scraped data source to the RAG chatbot, upsert the information into the vector store, and test it by asking questions about the content.

chapters.title: Conclusion and Limitations
chapters.description: This final chapter discusses the response from the RAG chatbot and covers the limitations of using open-source models, such as the lack of function calling.

summary:
## Why Use Ollama and Flowise?

- Build **free**, **local**, and **private** chatbots without relying on paid services like OpenAI.
- Run powerful open-source large language models (LLMs) like Llama 2, Mistral, and Mixtral directly on your own machine.

## Setting Up Ollama

1.  **Download and Install**: Get the installer from `ollama.com`.
2.  **Run an LLM Interactively**: Open your terminal and run a command like `olama run llama2`. This will download the model if it's your first time and allow you to chat with it directly.
3.  **Serve Ollama as an API**: To connect with Flowise, stop the interactive session (`Ctrl+D`) and run `olama serve`. This starts a local server, typically at `http://localhost:11434`.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> You must run a **local instance of Flowise** for it to connect to your local Ollama server. A cloud-hosted Flowise instance (like on Render) will not be able to access your machine's local services.

## Building a Simple Chatbot in Flowise

-   **Components**:
    -   `Conversational Chain`
    -   `ChatOlama` (Chat Model)
    -   `Buffer Memory` (Memory)
-   **ChatOlama Node Configuration**:
    -   **Base URL**: Use the default `http://localhost:11434`.
    -   **Model Name**: Specify the model you downloaded, e.g., `lama2`.

## Building a Local RAG Chatbot

This architecture allows the chatbot to answer questions based on your custom data.

-   **Components**:
    -   `Conversational Retrieval QA Chain`
    -   `ChatOlama` (Chat Model)
    -   `In-Memory Vector Store` (or another vector store like Pinecone)
    -   `Olama Embeddings` (Embeddings Model)
    -   `Cheerio Web Scraper` (Document Loader)

-   **Key Configuration Steps**:
    1.  **Olama Embeddings Node**: Use the same `Base URL` and `Model Name` (`lama2`) as your chat model.
    2.  **Data Source**: Add a document loader like the `Cheerio Web Scraper` and provide a URL.
    3.  **Upsert Data**: After saving the chat flow, click the **Upsert** button to scrape the data, create embeddings, and load it into the vector store.

> [!TIP]
> In the **Olama Embeddings** node, enable **"Use MMAP"** under "Additional Parameters." This may be required to prevent the upsert process from failing.

## Limitations of Open-Source Models

-   While powerful, many open-source models lack advanced features like **function calling**, which is a core component for creating complex agents with tools in platforms like OpenAI.
transcription:
## Introduction: Free Local Chatbots with Ollama

The OpenAI models that we use throughout this series are incredibly powerful, but they do come at a small cost. And sometimes all you need is a chatbot that runs on your local machine and that won't break the bank.\n\nIn this video, I will show you how you can build a RAG chatbot without spending any money using Flowwise and Olama.\n\nOlama is a tool that we can set up on our local machines and allows us to run LLM models locally. It also provides integration with many open source models like LLM2, Mistral, Mixtral and more. So in this video, I will show you how to set up Olama and then we'll download one of these models and we will then integrate Olama in Flowwise by first creating a simple conversation chain chatbot and lastly, we'll create a RAG chatbot that will scrape information from a website and we'll be able to ask questions about the content on that webpage.\n\nLet's start by setting up Olama.

## Installing and Running Your First Local LLM

To get started, go to olama.com, then click on download, then execute the file that you just downloaded and install Olama. So after installation, that installation pop-up will simply disappear, but that's actually expected and we will start Olama manually using the terminal. So on your machine, open the command prompt, PowerShell or terminal, whatever you prefer.\n\nAnd let's start by downloading our first model. The choice of model is extremely important as some of these models are extremely resource intensive. So for this video, I'm actually going to use the Llama 2 model, but of course, I recommend that you play with different models based on your hardware.\n\nIn order to download a model, you can simply click on the model name and on this page, we can see this command, `Olama run llama2`. Let's simply copy this command and let's run this in the terminal. The first time you run this, Olama will first download the Llama 2 model and you will then see this message saying, \"send a message\" and if I enter anything like \"hello\", I will get a response back from Llama 2.

## Serving Ollama for Flowise Integration

So there are actually a few ways to start up Olama and in this example, we simply started Olama using a specific model like Llama 2 and were able to chat with our model using the terminal, which is actually a lot of fun as well and very useful for testing out the responses from a given model. But in order to make this model available to Flow-wise, we'll actually use a different approach.\n\nSo to cancel out of this, I'm going to press Ctrl D. Now let's serve Olama as a local server by running `olama serve`. And by the way, if you ever receive this error message, it simply means that Olama is already running and you can actually confirm this by grabbing this URL and then opening it in the browser and you should see a message like this that says \"olama is running\".\n\nAnd Olama was actually already running on my machine. So I just quickly cancelled the previous session. So if we try this again by calling `olama serve`, this will now start an Olama server and listen for requests from Flow-wise. So now that we have Olama installed and running, let's create our chat flows in Flow-wise.\n\nNote that I am running a local instance of Flow-wise. So please ensure that you are also using a local instance if you are following along. An instance running on Render as example will not work as it will not have access to your local Olama instance. This video is very specifically intended for creating local chatbots on your own machine.

## Building a Basic Conversational Chatbot in Flowise

Let's create a new chat flow. Let's give it a name like \"local chatbot\". Let's save this and let's start by adding a chain. So under add nodes, go to chains and let's add the conversation chain. Let's add our chat model. So under chat models, let's add the chat Olama model. Let's connect this model to our chain and let's have a look at this chat Olama node.\n\nThis takes in a URL as input and this is the URL that our Olama instance is being served on. And if we copy this and open it in the browser, you should see this text saying \"olama is running\". If you do not see this text, then please ensure that you do have your Olama server running.\n\nIf that is working, we then have to specify our model name. And the model that we downloaded earlier was \"Lama2\". You are able to download multiple models using Olama. So if you have more than one type of model, you can easily swap them out using this field. Let's set the temperature to something like 0.7 and let's move on from that node. Let's add our memory node. So under add nodes, let's go to memory. I'm going to add the buffer memory node and let's connect that to our chain as well. And that is it. Let's save this chat flow. Let's test it out by saying something like \"hello\". And in less than a second, I got this response back from Olama. So we now have a completely free chat bot that we can use on our local machines.

## Building the Local RAG Chatbot Chain

So let's go ahead and create a RAG chat bot. This will allow us to upload a data source like a website address, PDF documents, text files, or whatever else we want. And we will then be able to ask the chat bot questions about that data.\n\nBut before we continue, if you enjoy this content, then please hit the like button, subscribe to my channel, and please let me know in the comments which open source models you prefer. Let's click on add. Let's save this. Let's call it \"local rag chat bot\". And let's save this.\n\nLet's start by adding a chain. So under add nodes, let's go to chains. And this time, let's add a conversational retrieval QA chain. This will allow us to add a data source to this chain. Let's add a chat model. So under chat models, let's go to chat Olama. Let's connect our model to the chain. Within the chat Olama node, let's set the model as \"Lama2\". And let's set the temperature to a lower value like 0.4.\n\nSo let's add our data source by adding a vector store retriever. So under add nodes, let's go down to vector stores. And I'm just going to use the in-memory vector store in this example. But feel free to use pinecone, chroma, or whatever you prefer. Let's connect our vector store to our chain. And now we need to add our embeddings model, which is also slightly different to what we're used to with openAI models. Let's go to add nodes. Then under embeddings, let's add the Olama embedding node. And let's connect this to our vector store. So for this node, we can leave the base URL the same as the base URL for the chat model. And for the model name, I will simply use \"Lama2\" as well. Then under additional parameters, I'm going to enable \"Use MMAP\". As I found that if I do not enable this, the upsert actually fails. This could be a bug, but at the moment, that is what seems to work for me. I'm going to close this popup, and let's go ahead and add our data source.

## Adding Data and Testing the RAG Chatbot

Let's click on add nodes. And under document loaders, you have the option of uploading a wide variety of different data sources. But for this video, I'm going to use the Cheerio web scraper in order to scrape information from a website. Let's attach this document loader to our vector store. And under URL, I'm simply going to use this link to the LangChain home page. So I'm going to copy this, and then paste it into this field. And that's pretty much all we have to do to set up our RAG chatbot. I'm going to save this chatbot. Let's upsert this information into the vector store. And now that that's done, we should be able to ask questions about that web page. So back in the chat, let's open this up, and let's ask, what is LangSmith?

## Conclusion and Limitations

And indeed, we do get the correct response back. Using these open source models can definitely be a lot of fun, but they do have their limitations. And as an example, it's very difficult to create an agent with tools using these open source models. As function calling is pretty much an open AI feature, let me know in the comments if you would like to see more videos using these open source models.
